sentences.headline: When 40% of flights are squeezed into two daily rush hours, the roster built for the normal timetable gets 85.1% of shipments ready on time. Re-planning the roster for the new schedule brings it back to 91.0% for 104 more staff hours a week.
sentences.flex: Keeping the recommended roster and adding a team of 4 on-call staff, called in whenever 60 or more shipments are waiting to be unpacked, does better still: 93.7% on time for 96 on-call hours a week.
sentences.volume: Even with 20% less freight, the recommended roster falls from 94.6% to 93.8% on time once 40% of flights bunch into rush hours.
sentences.timezone: Left unchecked, the time zone error alone moves on-time performance down 0.6 percentage points, from 93.5% to 92.9%.
sentences.catch: Flagging the riskiest 10% of shipments when their plane lands would catch 77% of the shipments that end up late.
sentences.drift: The early-warning model, trained on normal months, expects 14.3% of shipments to be late on the bunched schedule; in fact 16.9% are. It still puts the riskiest shipments first almost as well as before (ranking accuracy 0.959 on the normal timetable, 0.954 here), so its order holds but its odds need updating.
sentences.roster: On the normal timetable, a recommended roster gets 94.6% of shipments ready on time against 91.9% for the current roster, with 1,354 staff hours a week instead of 1,456.
